newsitem.title: USA: Miami sees surplus for 1997 but 96 still a mystery.
newsitem.headline: Miami sees surplus for 1997 but 96 still a mystery.

text.p: Miami projects a $6.5 million budget surplus for fiscal 1997, but still does not know how big a deficit it had in 1996, city officials said Tuesday in a budget session that a state official compared to "Alice in Wonderland."

The projected surplus is based on revenues and expenditures for the first quarter of fiscal 1997, which ended Dec. 31, 1996. City Manager Ed Marquez presented the data in a report to a state-appointed oversight board.
But the projection is also based on estimates that the city carried over a deficit of $19.4 million from fiscal 1996, which ended Sept. 30, 1996.

"I think the $19 million will change," Jose Rodriguez of KPMG Peat Marwick, the city's external auditor, told the board. Asked whether the deficit figure could rise or fall, Rodriguez replied, "I don't know."
The true size of the deficit will not be known until the firm completes its fiscal 1996 audit.
City workers, state budget experts and Peat Marwick auditors are still struggling to pin down actual figures from a budget the city previously conceded was "largely fiction."
Rodriguez said he was uncertain if the 1996 audit would be completed as scheduled March 31, even though the oversight board agreed to lend Miami five more state budget experts.
The audit deadline is just 15 days before the city is required to submit a five-year balanced budget to the board.
"We're building something on a foundation we're not sure about," the oversight board chairman, Lt. Gov. Buddy MacKay, said.
In a management letter submitted to city officials late Monday, Peat Marwick was sharply critical of Miami's accounting systems, noting that it failed to reconcile its accounts for months at a time.
"The completeness, accuracy and integrity of the city's accounting records cannot be relied upon by management to make informed financial and operating decisions," it said.
MacKay seemed to concur as Ed Marquez led the board through the city's first-quarter data.
"This is just like 'Alice in Wonderland'," MacKay said.

Gov. Lawton Chiles appointed the oversight board in December to guide Miami to fiscal solvency after a $68 million deficit was discovered in the city's original 1997 budget. The discovery came after three top city officials resigned to face federal corruption charges.
Last week the board approved a revised $275 million budget that eliminates the deficit, although that could change if the 1996 figures change significantly.
